_meta.description: B&B Shuffle card catalog. Normalized copy of every shared/decks/*/carddb.json plus deck metadata from Engine-V2/js/config.js. Organize by deck, then by card type. Card body/rule text is NOT stored in carddb.json for most decks (only core31 and green-expansion-v2 carry a 'description'); the authoritative full text lives on the card images (see card.image) and per-card reference links (see card.details). Scenario cards expose a 'detection' array = the Procedure cards printed in the card's DETECTION section (OCR'd from the card face into docs/card-detection.json). alignment.decks[*].scenarioNameAsProcedure lists scenario cards whose exact name also exists as a Procedure card — the name-level proxy for 'is this scenario card detectable by a procedure'. Use card.detection (procedure names) for the real scenario->procedure mapping; never rely on exact-name matching alone.

initial.name: Credential Stuffing
initial.description: The attackers used stolen username and password pairs (obtained from data breaches) and gained access to accounts on different systems.

initial.name: Exploited External Service
initial.description: The attackers targeted misconfigurations or unpatched vulnerabilities using publicly available exploits and gained access to your organization’s internal resources.

initial.name: Bring Your Own (Exploited) Device
initial.description: Your organization allows users to bring their own devices. The attackers compromised a user’s personal device to connect to your organization’s network.

initial.name: Social Engineering
initial.description: The attackers manipulated and deceived a user in your organization to bypass technical controls and gained access to sensitive information, credentials and/or systems.

initial.name: Compromised Trusted Relationship
initial.description: The attackers exploited a relationship between your organization and a third-party (e.g., vendor, partner, contractor) that has a service-level account within your organization and gained unauthorized access.

initial.name: External Password Spray
initial.description: The attackers gained access to your internal network by spraying commonly used passwords (like SeasonYear!) across multiple accounts.

initial.name: Insider Threat
initial.description: The attacker was a trusted individual who performed unauthorized actions within your organization.
detection: DLP (Ha! Ha! Kidding. DLP never works.)

initial.name: Unauthorized Cloud Access
initial.description: The attackers gained unauthorized access to your organization’s cloud infrastructure or Software as a Service (SaaS) applications.

initial.name: Compromised Web Server
initial.description: The attackers exploited vulnerabilities in an external web server to gain unauthorized access to your organizations internal network.

initial.name: Phishing
initial.description: The attackers gained access to your organization’s network through a deceptive email.

pivot.name: Local Privilege Escalation (LPE)
pivot.description: The attackers use a misconfiguration or vulnerability in local software to gain administrative access.

pivot.name: New Service Creation or Modification
pivot.description: The attackers create new services or modify existing ones to evade detection by launching malicious payloads at startup or altering legitimate services to execute unauthorized commands.

pivot.name: Credential Harvesting
pivot.description: The attackers collect and exploit username and password pairs found in open shares and files within your environment providing access to more valuable systems and data.

pivot.name: Weaponizing Active Directory
pivot.description: The attackers map Domain Trust Relationships, Group Policies, user/group privileges, and Object Access Control Lists (ACLs) in order to take full control of the Domain or network infrastructure.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Broadcast or Multicast Protocol Poisoning
pivot.description: The attackers exploit vulnerabilities in network protocols to intercept, redirect, or manipulate traffic to access sensitive data, impersonate devices, or disrupt communication.

pivot.name: Kerberoasting
pivot.description: The attackers compromise additional systems by using a “feature” of Service Principal Names (SPNs) to extract and crack service passwords.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

pivot.name: Internal Password Spray
pivot.description: The attackers enumerate accounts and spray commonly used passwords (like SeasonYear!) within the rest of your organization.
detection: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis

c2.name: Domain Fronting as C2
c2.description: The attackers route requests destined for their server through legitimate web services like Content Delivery Networks (CDNs).

c2.name: Cloud-Based Services as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use common cloud services to blend in with legitimate traffic to send sensitive data from a compromised system to their servers.

c2.name: Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use a legitimate service to send stolen data to a remote server.

c2.name: Domain Name System (DNS) as C2
c2.description: The attackers maintain communication with compromised systems and exfiltrate data using the standard DNS protocol.

c2.name: HTTPS as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use normal encrypted web ports and protocols to send stolen data from a compromised system to their servers.

c2.name: HTTP as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers use normal web ports and protocols to send stolen data from a compromised system to their servers.

persist.name: Accessibility Features
persist.description: The attacker hijack Operating System Accessibility features like Sticky Keys and On-Screen Keyboard.

persist.name: Malicious Firmware
persist.description: The attackers update the firmware of network cards, video cards, and Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) or Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) with malicious code, which allows them to survive reboots or operating system reinstalls, often evading detection.

persist.name: Logon Scripts
persist.description: The attackers add or modify scripts to your system’s logon process. This allows them to maintain access, escalate privileges, and perform malicious actions each time a user logs in.

persist.name: Malicious Browser Plugins
persist.description: The attackers install a browser plugin that executes malicious code and tracks activity while evading detection.

persist.name: Application Shimming
persist.description: The attackers use the Application Compatibility Toolkit (ACT) to trick applications into not seeing ports, directories, files, and services to evade detection.

persist.name: New User Added
persist.description: The attackers create a user account to maintain access  and ensure persistence, even if the original compromised account is discovered or disabled.

persist.name: Malicious Driver
persist.description: The attackers install or modify a device driver on a compromised system to retain control even after the system reboots.

persist.name: Dynamic Link Library (DLL) Hijacking
persist.description: The attackers inject malicious code into existing DLL files, often with elevated priveleges, to maintain access to the system even after it is rebooted.

persist.name: Malicious Service
persist.description: The attackers create or modify system services in order to maintain long-term access to a compromised system.

procedure.name: Permissions Audit
procedure.description: The Defenders examine configurations such as Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles in Microsoft Active Directory, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Azure AD permissions, or file access controls to detect excessive privileges, unauthorized access, or potential insider threats.

procedure.name: Cloud Event Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor, collect and examine event logs generated by cloud-based systems and services to identify potential security incidents, misconfigurations , and unusual or unauthorized activities.

procedure.name: Memory Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders pull the memory from the suspect system and review it for possible malicious activity, such as running malware, hidden processes, or unauthorized code execution.

procedure.name: Crisis Management
procedure.description: The Defenders coordinate response efforts during cybersecurity incidents, ensuring effective communication and swift containment.

procedure.name: Isolation
procedure.description: The Defenders quarantine compromised systems or network segments to prevent further spread of malicious activity, containing threats while enabling secure investigation and remediation.

procedure.name: Endpoint Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders investigate endpoint devices to identify indicators of compromise, unauthorized changes, or suspicious activities.

procedure.name: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
procedure.description: The Defenders leverage advanced analytics to detect anomalies in user behavior, identifying potential insider threats, compromised accounts, or unusual activity patterns.

procedure.name: Endpoint Security Protection Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders deploy and monitor endpoint security solutions to detect and prevent unauthorized access and activity on endpoints.

procedure.name: Active Defense and Cyber Deception
procedure.description: The Defenders simulate real systems and services, luring attackers to interact with them, carefully monitoring and alerting on those interactions.

procedure.name: Network Threat Hunting
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze network traffic to actively hunt for signs of malicious activity, such as unusual protocols, C2 communication, or data exfil.

procedure.name: Firewall Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders analyze logs generated by the firewall to monitor network traffic patterns, detect unauthorized access, and identify anomalies such as unusual connections or high traffic volumes.

procedure.name: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Log Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders use SIEM to aggregate logs from systems and devices to identify abnormal patterns, such as unusual access, traffic, or attack signatures.

procedure.name: Server Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders monitor sever activity, logs, and configurations to detect abnormal behaviors, such as unauthorized access, unusual traffic, or process anomalies.

procedure.name: Firewall Log Review
procedure.description: Can your organization analyze and understand firewall logs? Do you regularly emulate attack scenarios and verify that your procedures work?

procedure.name: Memory Analysis
procedure.description: The Defenders pull the memory from the suspect system and review it for possible malicious activity.

initial.name: Exploitation of Missing HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)
initial.description: The attackers exploited the lack of HSTS to force the victim’s browser to downgrade from HTTPS to HTTP, gaining login credentials, session cookies, or to inject malicious content into the user's browsing session.

initial.name: Supply Chain Attack
initial.description: The attackers inserted malware in the update process of one of your key enterprise management tools.

initial.name: Physical Access
initial.description: The attackers gained physical access to a system, device, or facility in your organization.

pivot.name: Server Message Block (SMB) Abuse
pivot.description: The attackers exploit vulnerabilities in the SMB protocol, which is commonly used for file and printer sharing across your network.

pivot.name: Internal Spearphishing
pivot.description: The attackers leverage existing access to a compromised user account to send attack emails that appear trustworthy to other users within the organization.

pivot.name: Access Token Manipulation
pivot.description: The attackers alter or forge authentication tokens to impersonate legitimate users, including administrators.

pivot.name: Stale Network Address Configurations (SNAC) Attack
pivot.description: The attackers exploit outdated or improperly cleaned-up network configurations such as old DNS, DHCP, or static IP entries that still reference decommissioned or reassigned systems.

pivot.name: Cleartext Passwords in Files
pivot.description: The attackers locate and extract unencrypted (plain text) passwords stored in configuration files, scripts, logs, or documents on a system.

c2.name: Physical Medium as Exfil
c2.description: The attackers leverage physical devices such as USB flash drives, smartphones, portable SSDs, and Raspberry Pi's to smuggle data out of your secured environments.

persist.name: Third-Party Malware Injection
persist.description: The attackers insert malicious code into software provided by a trusted third party such as libraries, plugins, or application updates which is then unknowingly distributed to end users or organizations.

persist.name: Malicious Email Rules
persist.description: The attackers create rules to a user's inbox to hide, redirect, or delete incoming messages to secretly control the flow of emails.

persist.name: Service Recovery Hijacking
persist.description: The attackers modify the recovery options of an existing service to execute malicious code when the service fails.

persist.name: Startup Registry Injection
persist.description: The attackers modify or create specific registry keys to ensure their malicious code runs automatically during system startup or user login.

procedure.name: Call a Consultant
procedure.description:
The Defenders hire an outside security consultant to help with the incident and uncover what your organization might have missed.

Choose one Consultant Card and add their modifier on this turn

procedure.name: Physical Security Review
procedure.description: The Defenders conduct a thorough review of badge systems, surveillance blind spots, unsecured entry points, and on-site access policies to uncover gaps that could be exploited by attackers.

procedure.name: Site Walkthrough
procedure.description: The Defenders send personnel to the site to examine the written logs, look for wireless access points, physical ingress methods, and equipment stacks to identify abnormalities.
